clue.text: 'Freed' city hospital taking old man! But there's a catch at first

indicators.note: says the catch comes at the front of the answer, before everything else
the hospital letter takes the old man straight after it, joining the two

parts.note: to bag something is to catch it, as a hunter bags game
a dad is a father, an old man in slang

explanation.surface: A sardonic jab at the 'liberation' of a city: its hospital takes in an old man, but there is a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'Freed' are Private Eye scorn for the 2003 claim that the Iraq invasion liberated the Iraqi capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Baghdad, capital of Iraq, was declared liberated by the US-led coalition in April 2003, hence the scare quotes.

clue.text: Hastings keen to give encouragement to the troops

parts.note: Hastings is the battle of 1066, so the place name stands for a battle
to keen is to wail or cry in grief

explanation.surface: The military historian Max Hastings is eager to cheer on the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Hastings reads as Max Hastings, the war correspondent, and keen as eager; really they are the 1066 battle and a verb for wailing.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle cry is the shout raised by soldiers to rouse themselves and their comrades as they go into action.

clue.text: Hit it off and assumed the mating position?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: formed a friendly relationship, got along well
second meaning: climbed on top, as one animal mounts another

explanation.surface: Two people who clicked and then went straight to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the saucy literal reading of a phrasal verb that normally means getting along.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both being on friendly terms with someone and, literally, climbing aboard, as in mounting.

clue.text: Horseshit collection from Brown: The Man Entering the Breach

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown colour

indicators.note: the man's letters go into the breach, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a breach is a gap in a wall or defence
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A jibe that Gordon Brown's output is a pile of nonsense, with the capitals dressing it like a book title.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like a title about Gordon Brown; Brown is only a colour here.
explanation.definitionFit: A dung heap is a pile of manure, a literal heap of droppings from horses and other animals.

clue.text: Had some tanked up editor

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used, a run lying inside them

parts.note: the run of letters sits across the end of tanked, all of up and the start of editor

explanation.surface: A drunken editor got a little of something, or had some of the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' as in 'I've been had': fooled.
explanation.definitionFit: To be had is slang for being cheated or tricked, which is exactly what being duped means.

clue.text: Almightily abandoned fire-fighter, not envious, accepts line

indicators.note: the line letter is taken in where one of the doubled letters stood
says the envious word is taken away from the fire engine

parts.note: a Green Goddess was the old army fire engine brought out during fire strikes
green is the colour of envy

explanation.surface: A fire-fighter left by the Almighty, free of envy, toes the line, a nod to the army's stand-in fire engines.
explanation.walkthrough: Green Goddesses were old army fire engines used in the 2002-3 firemen's strike. The clue does not say which letter makes way for the line, so this part is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone godless is without God, abandoned by the Almighty in the sense of lacking any faith or divine favour.

clue.text: When we 'never had it so good' with Glenda ego-tripping?

definitions.text: When we 'never had it so good'

indicators.note: Glenda and ego tripping over themselves stumble into a new order of letters

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words are the ones rearranged

explanation.surface: A dig at a vain Glenda, perhaps Glenda Jackson, in the boom years Macmillan boasted of.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Macmillan told Britons in 1957 that 'most of our people have never had it so good', and that era is the one in question.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden age is a period of peak prosperity, which Macmillan's late-1950s boast claimed Britain was living through.

clue.text: See 13
Former residence of Blair with small reduction for Brown's lot

parts.note: ex- is the prefix for former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: the small letter is cut away from the end of the residence's name

parts.note: Chequers is the country house used by British prime ministers, so Blair lived there
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Blair's old house gets cut down a bit before it goes to Gordon Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown was Blair's Chancellor of the Exchequer, the finance minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown ran the Treasury as Chancellor of the Exchequer, so the national finances were his responsibility, his lot.

clue.text: Barrage of insults "very restricting" — failed presidential candidate — "very"

indicators.note: the outer word restricts, holding the other letters inside it

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
Al Gore lost the 2000 US presidential election

explanation.surface: A torrent of abuse aimed at a losing presidential candidate, told in breathless quotes.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Gore was the Democratic candidate beaten by George W Bush in 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: A salvo is a simultaneous volley of gunfire, and figuratively a sudden burst of attacks or insults.

clue.text: God! Iain's first leader of Conservatives to jump ship!

indicators.note: these letters jump ship, leaving it

parts.note: the Titanic was the famous liner that sank in 1912

indicators.note: the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of Iain is the one leaving

indicators.note: the first letter of the following word leads it

parts.note: the first letter of Conservatives is the other one leaving

explanation.surface: Iain Duncan Smith, the first Tory leader to be ousted, is urged to abandon his sinking ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Iain Duncan Smith was Conservative leader in 2001-3, ousted before a general election; the Titanic is the sinking ship.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titans were the elder race of gods who ruled before the Olympians, so a Titan is a god.

clue.text: Controversial European — he's rejected by Jacko

parts.note: a Pole is a native of Poland, a European

indicators.note: the two letters of the pronoun he are thrown out of the name, each from its own place

parts.note: Jacko is the tabloid nickname of Michael Jackson

explanation.surface: Michael Jackson snubs some divisive European figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'he' leave the name separately, not as one block; the 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Polemical describes argumentative, contentious writing or speech, the kind that provokes heated dispute.

clue.text: Humped new head — made a meal of it

indicators.note: the first letter is swapped out for a different one, which only the crossing letters fix

parts.note: a humped back is a hunched one

explanation.surface: A hunchback gets a new head and then makes a big fuss over it.
explanation.walkthrough: The replacement first letter is not clued: crossings and the definition settle it. 'Made a meal of it' usually means overdoing something; here it is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To have lunched is literally to have eaten a midday meal, reading the idiom for fussing at face value.

clue.text: The old dauber, as the Spanish know Prince Philip?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old master painter, dauber being a mocking word for a painter

definitions.text: as the Spanish know Prince Philip
definitions.meaning: second meaning: 'the Greek', as Spaniards called a Greek, and Philip was born a prince of Greece

explanation.walkthrough: Prince Philip, the Queen's husband, was born Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, so he could be called 'the Greek'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cretan-born painter Doménikos Theotokópoulos worked in Toledo and was known to Spaniards by the nickname meaning the Greek.

clue.text: "Blasted civilians, getting in the way of US war aims," according to Pentagon?

definitions.meaning: literally civilians blown up by bombs, and also civilians cursed as a nuisance

definitions.text: getting in the way of US war aims
definitions.meaning: innocents who happen to be near a target, treated as an obstacle
the US military's own euphemism is what the clue is asking for

explanation.walkthrough: The Pentagon uses the phrase for civilians killed incidentally in an attack; the clue mocks it by making 'blasted' a curse as well as an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: The military euphemism refers to unintended deaths and destruction of civilians and property caused while striking a legitimate target.

clue.text: How some old Northerners got round Bolton gas explosion

definitions.text: How some old Northerners got round
definitions.note: the definition describes a means of travel, so it stands for the plural noun naming the vessels

indicators.note: a gas explosion blows the letters apart and they land in a new order

parts.note: the letters of the town and the fuel are the ones jumbled

explanation.surface: Elderly people from the North of England coping with a gas explosion in Bolton, a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Northerners' look like Lancashire pensioners, but they are the Vikings, Norsemen from the far north.
explanation.definitionFit: Vikings travelled the seas in long narrow oared ships, so these vessels were how the Norsemen got around.

clue.text: Creating peers makes Benn go barmy, holding back nothing

indicators.note: the jumbled letters hold the next piece inside them
barmy means crazy, so the letters go mad and rearrange

parts.note: the politician's surname and the verb supply the letters that get scrambled

indicators.note: the word for nothing is held backwards

parts.note: nil is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Tony Benn, who gave up his peerage, goes mad at the creation of new lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Benn fought to give up his inherited title as Viscount Stansgate, so making peers would infuriate him.
explanation.definitionFit: To ennoble someone is to raise them to the nobility, making them a peer of the realm with a title.

clue.text: Couple with a Liverpudlian accent sound content

indicators.note: in a Scouse accent the word for a couple is said with the vowel of fur

parts.note: a pair is a couple, two of something

explanation.surface: A Scouse couple whose talk makes a contented noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Scouse is the Liverpool accent, in which 'air' sounds like 'ur'. 'Content' here is the adjective, happy.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat purrs when it is happy, so the noise is the classic way to sound contented.

clue.text: Counsel, made to pay by judge, set new limits

parts.note: rede is an archaic word for advice or counsel
a judge who imposes a financial penalty has fined the defendant

explanation.surface: A barrister ordered by the judge to pay up, and boundaries are set again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counsel' looks like a barrister in court, but it is the old noun for advice.
explanation.definitionFit: To redefine a thing is to fix its scope or boundaries afresh, giving it new limits.

clue.text: Mugged twice? False

parts.note: two, the number of times
a mug is slang for a face, so mugged is jokingly read as faced

explanation.surface: Someone robbed twice, or a doubt over whether it really happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mugged' looks like robbed, but it is read as having a mug, a face.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-faced person is insincere and hypocritical, showing one face to you and another behind your back.

clue.text: American fighting machine needs new leader

indicators.note: the first letter is swapped for another, which the crossings fix

parts.note: a tank is an armoured fighting vehicle

explanation.surface: The American war machine needs someone new in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The new first letter is not clued, so the definition and crossings decide it.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is informal, often British, slang for a person from the United States.

clue.text: Prepared to have a bust up, being an inadequate bugger, maybe

definitions.text: Prepared to have a bust up
definitions.meaning: first meaning: of a bra, fitted with wire supports to lift the bust
second meaning: of a spy who plants listening devices, not fitted with enough wires

explanation.walkthrough: A bugger here is someone who plants bugs, hidden microphones; 'bust up' is lift, not a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Underwired bras have a wire sewn under each cup, and the word can be read as describing too little wiring.

clue.text: Times: "Brenda's a scrubber"

parts.note: eras are periods of time
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: The Times newspaper reporting that the Queen is a slattern.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls Queen Elizabeth 'Brenda', and ER is the royal cipher, Elizabeth Regina. Scrubber is British slang for a promiscuous woman.
explanation.definitionFit: An eraser rubs out marks, so it is literally a thing that scrubs, here taken apart from the slang insult.

clue.text: Rub up big vacuous bust of local dish

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are broken up and reformed

parts.note: both words are taken as written to be jumbled

indicators.note: an empty word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: with its middle emptied out only its outer letters remain

explanation.surface: Massaging a big, empty-headed chest, or the bust of a local beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub, and a dish is food, not a pretty person.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub grub is simple hearty food served in a British pub, and the local is one's neighbourhood pub.

clue.text: Publicly named a wanted individual, like a newspaper

definitions.meaning: first meaning: called out someone's name over a loudspeaker to summon them
second meaning: having pages, as a newspaper does

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanted individual' suggests a fugitive named in the press, but it is someone wanted on the phone at reception.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to summon them by announcement; anything made up of numbered sheets is described as having pages.

clue.text: Fan dancing? Get lost! Get lost!

indicators.note: the letters dance around into a new order

parts.note: the three letters of fan are the ones set dancing
eff off, written with the single letter, is a curt way of telling someone to get lost

explanation.surface: Someone tells a fan dancer twice over to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase was popularised by Princess Anne, reported as telling photographers to clear off; naff is British slang for tacky.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild British oath meaning go away, a minced version of a ruder expression.

clue.text: Sun's tip — 'The nation needs the like of Rebekah Wade' — bombed

indicators.note: the tip here is the end letter of the word

parts.note: the newspaper's name supplies just its end letter
the United Kingdom, abbreviated UK
Rebekah Wade edited the Sun, and ed is short for editor

explanation.surface: A Sun editorial claiming Britain needs more people like its editor, Rebekah Wade.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebekah Wade, later Brooks, edited the Sun newspaper from 2003.
explanation.definitionFit: To nuke a place is to attack it with nuclear weapons, so it has been bombed in the most extreme way.

clue.text: It sticks out transparently: there's nothing, that is, between Right and Left

parts.note: O looks like the digit zero

indicators.note: the Latin abbreviation goes between the two side letters

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that there is nothing at all between the political right and left.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a political complaint that the parties are all the same.
explanation.definitionFit: An oriel is a bay window projecting from an upper storey, glazed so it juts out from the wall and lets light through.

clue.text: As Reg, sportingly given credit for knob control

indicators.note: playing about in sport, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: these five letters are the ones rearranged
on tick means on credit

explanation.surface: A sporting Reg gets praise for, ahem, self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: Knob is innuendo; the knob is the top of a gear lever. 'Tick' for credit is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's gearstick is the lever topped by a knob that controls which gear is engaged.

clue.text: A stoned heap, one's coupled with Archer finally in prison

indicators.note: the paired letters sit in the prison word

parts.note: the can is slang for prison

indicators.note: the numeral is paired with the next letter, placed side by side

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one; the 's is a link

indicators.note: only the final letter of the name is used

parts.note: the last letter of the disgraced novelist's surname

explanation.surface: A drug-addled wreck shares a cell with Jeffrey Archer, at last in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury in 2001. 'Stoned' looks like high on drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A cairn is a mound of piled-up stones built as a landmark or memorial, so literally a heap made of stones.

clue.text: The cleaner of two ways to get e.g. Rupert Murdoch's media fare

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a cloth for wiping away dust
second meaning: a rubbish newspaper, a rag only fit for the dustbin

explanation.walkthrough: A rag is a low-quality newspaper; Private Eye readily applies it to Murdoch's Sun and News of the World. 'Of two ways to get' says the phrase is read two ways.
explanation.definitionFit: A duster is a soft cloth for wiping surfaces clean, and a rag is a scornful word for a trashy paper.

clue.text: Pissed model giving way to date, was a cheat

indicators.note: the model letter makes way for the date letter, which replaces it

parts.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and tiddled means tipsy
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so T stands for model

explanation.surface: A drunken model gives up her place to a date, having been unfaithful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British for drunk, not American for angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To diddle someone is to swindle them, so one who diddled was a cheat.
